scopeReview: IMP-2.D.1–2: slavery/forced departure, refugees/asylum seekers/IDPs and transnational, transhumance, internal, chain, step, guest-worker, rural–urban types. Distinguishes overlapping geographic dimensions, compulsion and administrative status. No actual eligibility decisions or national legal advice.
varietyReview: Border-crossing flow map, case table, staged settlement model and seasonal household chart. Additional historical, labor, network, transnational and mixed-choice scenarios plus recognition arithmetic. All five skills and varied difficulty/keys.
repetitionReview: Unlike2.10 driver questions, these identify movement types using required facts. Step/network tasks contrast one household’s stages with linked households; temporal pastoral cycles differ from permanent labor moves. Border map assesses route categories rather than net flow arithmetic.
referenceNote: Primary institutional definitions checked for internal/cross-border and pending/recognized distinctions; pending applicants may meet refugee criteria before recognition. All cases/numbers/figures original. No current legal determination, copied lesson questions, external catalog addition or human review claim.

questions.correctOption: The 600 who remain in A are internally displaced; the 400 entering B are cross-border displaced, with refugee criteria requiring further assessment.
questions.independentReview: Checked internal path endpointsx10/40 remain below borderx50; cross-border path endsx75 in B. Counts600+400=1000. Violence supplies forced departure; exact refugee eligibility/procedure is deliberately not inferred from arrows alone.

questions.correctOption: A is an asylum-seeker with a pending claim; B has formal refugee recognition; C is internally displaced.
questions.independentReview: Read A pending/B recognized/C same-country flood separately. Formal recognition is declaratory rather than what creates a refugee’s underlying circumstances; no claim that a pending person cannot already be a refugee.

questions.correctOption: Step migration through successive settlement stages.
questions.independentReview: Followed the same household acrossVillage→Town→City and distinct2020/2023 move labels. Verified sequential settlement stages, while no family-predecessor or seasonal-return mechanism is present.

questions.correctOption: Transhumance, involving seasonal movement between grazing areas.
questions.independentReview: Verified lowland/highland totals30 at every season and winter30/0 versus summer0/30. Counts alone would not identify pastoral purpose; that purpose and annual return are explicitly provided.

questions.correctOption: The movement is compelled rather than a freely chosen relocation.
questions.independentReview: Identified compelled movement as the essential distinction in the supplied historical scenario. Avoided treating all labor migration as slavery or making any unverified route/count claim about a particular historical episode.

questions.correctOption: A guest-worker arrangement, which does not by itself establish permanent settlement.
questions.independentReview: Matched explicit voluntary fixed-period cross-border labor admission to the program type. Did not infer a real visa entitlement, later residence outcome, coercion or asylum claim.

questions.correctOption: Chain migration supported by a social network.
questions.independentReview: Traced the link between predecessor migrants’ assistance and later arrivals. Distinguished a network of separate movers from one household’s staged path, and avoided inferring force from kinship.
Checked country-boundary and settlement-type dimensions independently. Both can be true simultaneously without assigning a legal category or a mechanism not given in the scenario.

questions.correctOption: Transnational migration and social connections spanning more than one country.
questions.independentReview: Identified sustained multi-country activities rather than simply international location. No unsupported assertion about dual citizenship, legal residence or universal migrant behavior is made.

questions.correctOption: Destination alone does not establish the degree of choice or compulsion behind a move.
questions.independentReview: Held destination constant while varying the stated departure circumstances. Therefore endpoint cannot identify coercion; no legal refugee determination or claim that all migration fits a perfectly binary choice is inferred.

questions.correctOption: Forty percent have received formal recognition so far; pending cases are not reported decisions.
questions.independentReview: Independently calculated200/500=.4 and checked200+300=500 with no other outcomes. Interpretation is limited to reported recognition procedures, not a claim that recognition creates refugee circumstances or that pending applicants are unprotected.
